article.title: Using XSLT
article.p: This section describes how to use XSLT stylesheets with SaxonC, either from the command line, from the C/C++ API or Python API, or from PHP:
For details on Compiling a stylesheet, and Performance analysis you wil find in the main Saxon documentation.
Furthermore, a summary description of the current Saxon implementation of XSLT 3.0 is provided, with links to other relevant sections of the documentation.
For full information about the conformance of Saxon to the XSLT 3.0 specification, and about the handling of implementation-defined features of the specifications, see Conformance.

section.title: From the command line
section.p: See instructions and options available for running SaxonC from the command line in the section command line option of the main Saxon documentation.

section.title: From a C application
section.h1: XSLT transformations from a C application
section.p: In this section we give a tutorial of how to setup a C API application. In SaxonCProcessor.h we have several functions to execute XSLT stylesheets. Please note the compile phase happens within the same execute function call. There are functions to output the results to file or string representation. The XML document sources and execution file are supplied as arguments to the function, but users may find it useful to supply parameters and properties using the structs sxnc_parameter and sxnc_property, respectively.
The first step is the memory allocation of the processor and variables required by SaxonC. To simplify the process we have the utility function initSaxonc() to alloc the following variables:

ul.li: environ - SaxonC environment given as the struct sxnc_environment
processor - The SaxonC Processor data structure given as the struct sxnc_processor which is used as a reference to the Java Saxon Processor object in Java

parameters - The sxnc_parameter struct as an array is used to represent the the parameters required by the XSLT processors. For example stylesheet parameters can be supplied here. See further details here.
properties - The sxnc_property struct as an array is used to represent the properties required by the XSLT processors. See full list of properties here.

section.title: From a C++ application
section.h1: XSLT transformations from a C++ application
section.p: Rather than running XSLT transformations from the command line, you may want to invoke transformations from your own C++ application. If you use Saxon repeatedly to perform multiple transformations, this will always be much faster than running it each time from a command line.
The C++ API is the core API for SaxonC upon which the Python and PHP APIs are built.
You can perform a transformation using the C++ interface as follows:

li.p: Create a SaxonProcessor and set any global configuration options on the SaxonProcessor object. If your stylesheet uses any features that require SaxonC-PE or SaxonC-EE, be sure to use the constructor new SaxonProcessor(true).
Call newXslt30Processor() to create an Xslt30Processor, and set any options that are local to a specific compilation (for example, the destination of error messages).
li.aside: Error messages that occur during the compile phase are handled internally in SaxonC and thrown as the C++ exception SaxonApiException. throwing exceptions is fine for an application run from a console, but not so good if it's executing on a web server, or behind a graphical interface. In such cases you'll want to catch the exception and handling it accordingly.

li.p: Call the compileFromFile() or compileFromString() or compileFromAssociatedFile() method to compile a stylesheet. The result is a pointer to the XsltExecutable object, which can be used as often as you like, in the same thread or in different threads.

It is also possible to run the one shot transformations transformFileToString() and transformFileToFile() on the Xslt30Processor, but these methods have limited features and are not designed for XSLT 3.0. For XSLT 3.0 it is advisable to use one of the compile methods above to create a XsltExecutable.

To run a transformation, there are methods available on the XsltExecutable to execute a compiled stylesheet. For example, invoking the xsl:apply-template has three methods available applyTemplatesReturningString(), applyTemplatesReturningValue() and applyTemplatesReturningFile(). As the name suggest these methods returns the output of the stylesheet as a serialized string given a char pointer array, pointer to XdmValue object and file on disk, respectively. There are other methods such as call function and call template name.

The XsltExecutable class was introduced in SaxonC 11.1, it provides new ways of executing stylesheet code that are defined in the XSLT 3.0 specification, though Saxon also allows you to use the same entry points with 1.0 or 2.0 stylesheets. Among the new capabilities are:

ul.li: You can invoke a specific stylesheet function, with parameters, rather than invoking a named template or template rule.

If you start execution with a named template or template rule, you can supply values for the parameters defined on that template, as well as the global stylesheet parameters using the setParameter() method. The SaxonProcessor has a number of utility methods to create Xdm objects (for example makeStringValue() to create an XdmAtomicValue object from a char pointer array).
Details of options available properties and parameters and how to use them you can find here: Configuration.

Whether you execute a template or a function, you can return the results in raw string as a char pointer array, to file or as an XDM type. For example, a function (or template) might return a sequence of strings, or a single boolean, or a map, or even a function.

It is possible to capture the secondary result documents into an std:map (as the pair URI key and XdmNode) using the setCaptureResultDocuments. This override the default mechanism of writing the result documents to file. To retrieve the result documents the method getResultDocuments() is to be called after the execution of the stylesheet.

There is no longer any necessary relationship between the "principal source document" (if it still exists) and the context item for evaluating global variables. The two things are quite independent of each other. The SaxonProcessor provides methods for parsing XML documents from file and from a string literal (e.g parseXmlFromFile()). The DocumentBuilder class is more feature rich to parse XML documents such as setting a SchemaValidator.

The source document can be set on the XsltExecutable via the methods setInitialMatchSelection() and setInitialMatchSelectionAsFile(). It is sometimes a requirement to supply the context item to be used when evaluating global variables and parameters. This we would do using the setGlobalContextItem() or setGlobalContextFromFile()

section.title: From a Python application
section.h1: XSLT transformations from a Python application
section.p: This guide is for using SaxonC in a Python application.
You can perform a transformation using the Python interface as follows:

li.p: Create a PySaxonProcessor and set any global configuration options on the PySaxonProcessor object. If your stylesheet uses any features that require saxoncpe or saxoncee, be sure to use the constructor proc = PySaxonProcessor(license=False).
Call new_xslt30_processor() to create an PyXslt30Processor, and set any options that are local to a specific compilation (for example, the destination of error messages).
li.aside: Error messages that occur during the compile phase are handled internally in SaxonC and thrown as Python exception PySaxonApiError. throwing exceptions is fine for an application run from a console, but not so good if it's executing on a web server, or behind a graphical interface. In such cases you'll want to catch the exception and handling it accordingly.

li.p: Call the compile_stylesheet() method to compile a stylesheet. The result is a pointer to the PyXsltExecutable object, which can be used as often as you like, in the same thread or in different threads.

It is also possible to run the one shot transformations transform_to_string() and transform_to_file() on the PyXslt30Processor, but these methods have limited features and are not designed for XSLT 3.0. For XSLT 3.0 it is advisable to use one of the compile methods above to create a PyXsltExecutable.

To run a transformation, there are several methods available on the XsltExecutable to execute a compiled stylesheet. For example, invoking the xsl:apply-template has three methods available apply_templates_returning_string(), apply_templates_returning_value() and apply_templates_returning_file(). As the name suggest these methods returns the output of the stylesheet as a serialized string (str), PyXdmValue object and file on disk, respectively. There are other methods such as call function and call template name.

The PyXsltExecutable class was introduced in SaxonC 11.1, it provides new ways of executing stylesheet code that are defined in the XSLT 3.0 specification, though Saxon also allows you to use the same entry points with 1.0 or 2.0 stylesheets. Among the new capabilities are:

ul.li: You can invoke a specific stylesheet function, with parameters, rather than invoking a named template or template rule.

If you start execution with a named template or template rule, you can supply values for the parameters defined on that template, as well as the global stylesheet parameters using the set_parameter() method.
Details of options available properties and parameters and how to use them you can find here: Configuration.

Whether you execute a template or a function, you can return the results in raw string as a char pointer array, to file or as an XDM type. For example, a function (or template) might return a sequence of strings, or a single boolean, or a map, or even a function.

It is possible to capture the secondary result documents into an std:map (as the pair URI key and PyXdmNode) using the set_capture_result_documents(). This override the default mechanism of writing the result documents to file. To retrieve the result documents the method get_result_documents() is to be called after the execution of the stylesheet.

There is no longer any necessary relationship between the "principal source document" (if it still exists) and the context item for evaluating global variables. The two things are quite independent of each other. The PySaxonProcessor provides simple methods for parsing XML documents from file and from a string literal (e.g parse_xml()). The PyDocumentBuilder class is more feature rich with options to parse a XML document such as setting a PySchemaValidator

The source document can be set on the PyXsltExecutable via the methods set_initial_match_selection() which has the keyword arguments file_name|xdm_value. It is sometimes a requirement to supply the context item to be used when evaluating global variables and parameters. This we would do using the set_global_context_item().

section.title: Handling output
section.p: General information of the output produced by a stylesheet is discussed in the section Handling stylesheet output of the main Saxon documentation.
In SaxonC, the mechanism for controlling where the stylesheet output is sent and how it formatted is different to the other Saxon product therefore we discuss it here:

section.title: Principal output
section.p: When a transformation is run from the command line, the destination of the principal output is given by the -o option, and defaults to the standard output stream (that is, the console). The output is always serialized; the format of the serialization is determined by xsl:output declarations within the stylesheet itself, or by options such as !indent=yes on the command line. Command line options take precedence.
When running from an application, the destination of the principal output is controlled using the API:

ul.li: In the C API transformation output is returned as serialized string (pointer to a char array) or send to a specified file.

li.p: In the C++, Python and PHP APIs, transformation there a multiple methods to handle the output. These methods have the naming convention of [prefix]ReturningValue, [prefix]ReturningString and [prefix]ReturningFile. Please note for Python we use underscore in the method name (e.g [prefix]_returning_value).
The output can be returned a serialized string (pointer to a char array) or send to a specified file.

You can capture the raw output of the transformation as an XdmValue, for example, callTemplateReturningValue. In some cases the value is returned as one of the sub-classes of XdmValue: (i.e. XdmItem, XdmNode, XdmAtomicValue, XdmFunctionItem, XdmArray or XdmMap). This can be done using the method setResultAsRawValue()
All other options produce tree output, namely XdmNode.
If you want to perform further processing on the output, you can send it to a SchemaValidator for validation, or to an XsltExecutable for further transformation.

section.title: Secondary output
section.p: The term secondary output refers to values produced using the xsl:result-document instruction. As with the principal output, applications can control both the destination of secondary output, and its format.

When running from the command line, secondary outputs are always serialized, using the serialization parameters supplied on the xsl:result-document instruction itself, or in the xsl:output declaration referenced in its format attribute. Serialization parameters supplied on the command line (for example !indent=yes) only take effect if the xsl:result-document chooses to use the default output format.

By default, secondary outputs are written to a file whose name is established by resolving the relative URI given in the @href attribute of xsl:result-document against the base output URI of the transformation. The base output URI defaults to the destination of the principal output.
The destination and format of secondary outputs can be influenced using the C++, Python and PHP APIs:

li.p: The SaxonC APIs on the XsltExecutable, have a method setCaptureResultDocuments() which accepts two boolean flags: first argument is a flag where the value true enables the capturing of in a map (std::map< std::string, XdmValue * >). The second argument is to switch on results as raw results. After executing the transformation we call getResultDocuments() to return the map. The string in the map is the document URI. The default is to send secondary documents to file storage. In PHP we return the getResultDocuments() returns the map as a XdmMap. In Python the get_result_documents() returns a Python dict (i.e. dict [str, PyXdmValue]). For example in Python we would do the following:

section.p: In the case of an xsl:result-document instruction with no href attribute, the output is sent to the principal output destination, which must not then be used for anything else. The main reason for this is to allow serialization options to be set dynamically.

Because xsl:result-document is an instruction that by its nature has side-effects, which runs against the grain of XSLT's pure functional language philosophy, the XSLT specification defines a number of rules constraining what the instruction can do. Notably (a) you can't write more than one output to the same URI, and (b) you can't write to a URI that the transformation also reads from.

SaxonC-EE evaluates the xsl:result-document instruction asynchronously, unless multi-threading is explicitly disabled. This means that the transformation might be building several output files in parallel. This will cause problems if the stylesheet uses extension functions that have side-effects.

section.title: Message output
section.p: XSLT defines the xsl:message instruction to produce output, but leaves nearly all details of its behaviour implementation-defined. Although the content of a message is often a simple text string, the specification defines it as an XML document fragment. By default Saxon serializes this document and writes it to the standard error stream. The serialization is done with method="xml" indent="yes" omit-xml-declaration="yes".

div.p: A SaxonC application can customize the handling of xsl:message output by calling the setSaveXslMessage(bool show, const char* filename = nullptr) method on the XsltExecutable. This applies to the APIs on C++, Python and PHP. The first argument on the method is to enable the output of the xsl:message to the standard output error listener. Default is on. The second argument is to switch on the output of xsl:message to file Each message is appended at the end of the file. We can retrieve the xsl:message's using the getXslMessages() to return sequence of messages as XdmItems in the XdmValue, for example:
